2 Discrete Wavelet Transform for Telematics Signals
Inthis section, wedevelopatrip-level representationthatwillserve asinputtoour proposedriskindex.
For each trip, we decompose the signal into wavelet coefficients across multiple time scales and then
aggregate these coefficients into a single series that summarizes driving patterns over both short and
long durations. The resulting aggregated series is used to form an input portfolio distribution, which
is a key ingredient of the proposed risk index in the subsequent sections. As discussed in Section 1,
this representation applies to any telematics signal recorded as a time series and can be extended to a
multivariate risk index that integrates multiple telematics signals in future work.
To achieve this, we employ awavelet transformPercival and Walden (2013), which is particularly
wellsuitedfordetectingabnormalpatternsintelematicssignalsacrossmultipletimescales. Telematics
signals typically exhibit abrupt, short-lived events (e.g., harsh braking or acceleration), making global or
overly smooth representations less effective. For example, Fourier bases have global support over the
entireobservationwindowandB-splinebasesimposesmoothness. Incontrast,waveletsareexplicitly
designedtocapturelocalizedfeaturesintime: waveletbasesarelocalizedintimeandoperatethrough
filters of varying duration, from short to long scales, that concentrate around points of change. The
resulting wavelet coefficients are therefore associated with specific time intervals and scales, enabling
precise identificationof transientbehaviors. This localizationpropertymakesthe wavelet transform a

naturalandeffectiverepresentationforanalyzingtelematicssignalsandextractingrisk-relevantdriving
patterns.
In this paper, we use themaximal overlap discrete wavelet transform(MODWT) rather than a regular
discrete wavelet transform (DWT) because it is a better choice for telematics signals when our goal is
to detect abnormal driving behavior while retainingallpossible features that could later be identified
as abnormal patterns. Since the regular DWT does downsampling, it critically depends on where we
“break into” the series, i.e., what we take as a starting point or origin for analysis. In other words, the
regular DWT is sensitive to shifts so its filter might not line up well with interesting features in a time
seriesPercivalandWalden(2013). Incontrast,asyoumayhavealreadynoticedbytheterm“maximal
overlap”,theMODWTappliesthewaveletandscalingfiltersateverytimepointthroughcircularshifts,
considering all possible placements of the filters with the signal. This prevents missing important driving
behaviors that occur at arbitrary times within a trip because the MODWT produces coefficients at every
time point without downsampling.
We now formalize this representation by defining the MODWT filters and the resulting wavelet
and scalingcoefficients for each trip. These coefficients willbe aggregated to form the input portfolio

6 Conclusion and Further Work
This paper proposes a frequency–severity joint trip- and driver-level risk index for telematics signals,

learn a stable portfolio baseline and translate tail rarity into an interpretable severity scale that can be
combined with trip-level tail frequencies.
Our main contributions are threefold. First, we formalize a portfolio-level notion of severity for
telematics-based ratemaking by treating extreme tail behaviors as the risk-relevant events. Second,
we extend the existing single-Uniform Gaussian–Uniform formulation to a multi-Uniform layered tail
structure and develop the MU-MEMR fitting procedure to make likelihood-based estimation feasible
under multiple tail layers. Third, the fitted layers induce multi-layer tail counts (MLTCs) that admit a
conjugatePoisson–Gammafrequencymodel,yieldingaclosed-formper-exposureriskindexandenabling
sequential updating to construct dynamically evolving driver-level risk profiles.
In the UAH-DriveSet controlled study, the fitted severity model provides a robust separation between
typical (Gaussian) dynamics and abnormal (Uniform) tail behaviors, which makes it coherent to penalize
the driving patterns based on their own extremeness in risk evaluation. Empirically, MLTC layering
clarifies why total tail counts alone can be misleading, while the severity-weighted index produces
consistent separation between normalandriskytrips and supports coherent ranking and updating
at the driver level. The accompanying binary classification study further validates that incorporating
portfolio-level severity weights improves discrimination, compared with other two frequency-based
models (Model A and B).

structure.title: Preface
structure.summary:
This partial document introduces a novel risk index for assessing driver and trip risk using telematics data. The core innovation is a "frequency-severity joint trip-level risk index" that combines the frequency of abnormal driving patterns with a severity component that quantifies how extreme these behaviors are relative to a portfolio-level baseline.

Key points covered include:

*   **Novel Risk Index:** A new index is proposed that jointly considers the frequency and severity of abnormal driving patterns.
*   **Severity Quantification:** Severity is measured through an inverse-probability penalty, emphasizing the rarity of extreme tail behaviors rather than claim size.
*   **Data Processing:** High-frequency telematics data, specifically longitudinal acceleration, is processed using the Maximal Overlap Discrete Wavelet Transform (MODWT) to capture localized driving patterns across multiple time scales.
*   **Portfolio Distribution Modeling:** A Gaussian-Uniform mixture model with a layered tail structure is used to model the portfolio distribution, distinguishing typical driving behavior from increasingly extreme tail behaviors.
*   **Risk Index Construction:** Multi-layer tail counts (MLTC) are constructed at the trip level and modeled within a Poisson-Gamma framework to derive a closed-form posterior risk index that reflects both frequency and severity.
*   **Dynamic Risk Profiles:** The conjugate structure of the model allows for sequential updating, enabling the creation of dynamically evolving driver-level risk profiles.
*   **Application and Validation:** The proposed index is demonstrated using the UAH-DriveSet controlled dataset to show its ability to discriminate between driving states, identify high-risk trips, and rank drivers, offering a behavior-driven risk measure for actuarial applications.
*   **Motivation for Severity:** The document highlights the limitations of traditional static driver/vehicle characteristics in capturing real-time behavior and argues for the necessity of incorporating behavioral severity alongside frequency for a more comprehensive risk assessment.
*   **Dataset Description:** The UAH-DriveSet, a public smartphone-sensor dataset, is described, including details about drivers, vehicles, driving states (normal, aggressive, drowsy), routes, and the focus on longitudinal acceleration data.

nodes.title: Preliminary Analysis:
nodes.summary:
The provided document excerpt focuses on developing a novel risk index for evaluating driving behavior using telematics signals. The main points covered are:

*   **Limitations of Traditional Frequency-Based Analysis:** The preliminary analysis highlights that simply counting occurrences of abnormal events (e.g., exceeding a single acceleration threshold) can be misleading. A "normal-looking" distribution of longitudinal acceleration might mask underlying risky behavior, especially in the tails of the distribution.
*   **Introduction of Severity Layers:** To address this, the document proposes incorporating "severity layers" by examining deeper quantiles of the distribution. This allows for a more granular understanding of abnormal patterns, where events in more extreme tails are considered more severe.
*   **Development of a Frequency-Severity Joint Risk Index:** The core objective is to construct a risk index that jointly accounts for both the frequency and severity of abnormal driving behaviors. This index aims to identify dangerous trips and high-risk drivers without relying on traditional covariates like claims data.
*   **Signal Representation using Wavelet Transform:** Telematics signals are represented using the Maximal Overlap Discrete Wavelet Transform (MODWT) to capture localized patterns across multiple time scales. These coefficients are aggregated to create a trip-level summary.
*   **Portfolio-Level Severity Model:** A Gaussian-Uniform mixture model is used to define abnormal tail behavior at the portfolio level, ensuring comparability across trips and drivers.
*   **Trip-Level Frequency Model and Risk Index Calculation:** Layer-wise trip counts are modeled using a Poisson-Gamma structure, and the final risk index is calculated as a severity-weighted per-exposure risk rate.
*   **Applications and Benefits:** The proposed index functions as an anomaly index, providing a per-exposure trip score for insurance applications (pricing, underwriting) and for transportation safety and fleet management (prioritizing review and intervention). It is particularly useful when claims data is sparse.
*   **Future Work:** The framework is signal-agnostic and can be extended to multivariate settings by combining multiple telematics signals.

structure.title: Discrete Wavelet Transform for Telematics Signals:
structure.summary:
This partial document describes a framework for analyzing telematics signals to assess driving risk. The main points covered are:

*   **Severity and Frequency Modeling:**
    *   A Gaussian–Uniform mixture model is used to estimate the severity of abnormal driving behaviors, with Gaussian components representing typical behavior and Uniform components capturing abnormal tail behavior.
    *   Trip-level frequency is modeled using a Poisson–Gamma structure for trip counts.
    *   A risk index is defined as a severity-weighted per-exposure risk rate, which can be updated sequentially to create dynamic driver profiles.

*   **Focus on Longitudinal Acceleration:**
    *   The framework deliberately focuses on longitudinal acceleration due to its established relevance in detecting risky driving behavior.
    *   The framework is signal-agnostic and can be applied to other telematics responses.

*   **Wavelet Transform for Signal Representation:**
    *   The Maximal Overlap Discrete Wavelet Transform (MODWT) is employed to decompose telematics signals into wavelet coefficients across multiple time scales.
    *   MODWT is chosen over the regular DWT because it is better suited for detecting abnormal patterns in telematics signals by applying filters at every time point without downsampling, thus retaining all possible features.
    *   The Daubechies D4 wavelet filter is specifically adopted for its ability to capture the mean-reversion characteristic of telematics signals and avoid underestimating localized deviations.
    *   The resulting aggregated wavelet coefficients form an input portfolio distribution for severity and frequency modeling.

*   **Applications of the Risk Index:**
    *   The index functions as an anomaly index, accounting for both frequency and severity of abnormal behaviors.
    *   In insurance, it provides a per-exposure trip score for pricing and underwriting in Usage-Based Insurance (UBI).
    *   In transportation safety and fleet management, it can prioritize reviews and interventions.
    *   It serves as a signal-based screening metric, even with limited claims data.

*   **Paper Structure:**
    *   The document outlines the organization of the paper, including sections on MODWT representation, severity modeling, frequency modeling, empirical application, and future directions.

structure.title: Severity Model:
structure.summary:
The provided document excerpt details two main sections: "Across-level Aggregation" and "Severity Model".

The "Across-level Aggregation" section explains a method for combining wavelet coefficients from different time scales within a trip into a single time series. This aggregation aims to capture both short-term and long-term driving patterns. It defines an aggregated wavelet coefficient ($C_{i,t}$) and presents several practical aggregation functions, including maximum, average pooling, weighted pooling, and single-level choice. The resulting aggregated time series ($C_i$) is intended to summarize driving behaviors across multiple temporal scales and will serve as an input for subsequent risk modeling.

The "Severity Model" section focuses on modeling the distribution of driving behaviors at a portfolio level to establish a stable baseline for risk evaluation. It addresses the limitations of purely Gaussian models for longitudinal acceleration, which can be distorted by extreme values. The proposed solution is a Gaussian-Uniform mixture model that separates typical driving (Gaussian component) from abnormal tail behavior (Uniform components). This approach aims to create a more robust reference distribution for severity modeling, less influenced by specific driving styles or portfolio composition. The document introduces a novel "Multi-Uniform MEMR (MU-MEMR)" algorithm, extending existing methods to handle multiple Uniform components. This algorithm allows for the quantification of severity based on the rarity of driving patterns. The section also discusses the construction of a portfolio distribution using a hierarchical sampling and within-trip thinning scheme to address potential issues like noise and temporal dependencies within trips. Finally, it outlines the likelihood function and parameter estimation for this mixture model, detailing the use of latent variables and the Expectation-Maximization (EM) algorithm. The MU-MEMR algorithm is further elaborated, including initialization strategies using trimmed k-means and the definition of base grids for Uniform components.

nodes.title: Multi-Uniform MEMR Algorithm:
nodes.summary:
The provided document excerpt focuses on a statistical modeling approach, specifically the Multi-Uniform MEMR (MU-MEMR) algorithm, and its application in risk assessment.

The main points covered are:

*   **EM Formulation and Decomposition:** The document begins by presenting the Expectation-Maximization (EM) formulation, which is then decomposed into four distinct components: $Q_{u^-}$, $Q_{\phi}$, $Q_{u^+}$, and $Q_{\pi}$. This suggests a structured approach to parameter estimation within the EM framework.

*   **MU-MEMR Algorithm Description:** A significant portion details the MU-MEMR algorithm, highlighting its key difference from a standard MEMR approach: the structure of tail layers. It involves splitting tails into partitions, selecting tail layers, reinitializing Uniform parameters, and running EM for Gaussian components and membership probabilities. This process is described as a candidate search making EM fitting feasible for Gaussian-Uniform mixtures.

*   **Robust Initialization:** The algorithm employs trimmed-k-means for robust initialization of Gaussian components, which is less affected by extreme values. This also provides a base grid for candidate search for Uniform parameters.

*   **Base Grid for Uniform Components:** The process of defining a base grid for Uniform components is explained, involving splitting intervals based on trimmed observations and setting split points to nearest observed values.

*   **Parameter Space Constraints:** To ensure stable estimation and interpretable severity structure, the Gaussian-Uniform mixture parameters are restricted by four constraints:
    *   **Scale Constraint:** To avoid degenerate fits by bounding component scales (e.g., $\sigma_g \to 0$ or $u_{m+1} \to u_m$).
    *   **Tail-Separation Constraint:** To keep Uniform tails separated from Gaussian cores.
    *   **Tail Coverage Constraint:** To ensure Uniform supports cover the full tail range with consecutive intervals.
    *   **Monotonicity Constraint:** To enforce non-increasing membership probabilities for Uniform components in deeper tail layers, indicating higher severity.

*   **Constrained Maximum-Likelihood Estimator:** The document defines the constrained parameter space and the objective of finding the constrained maximum-likelihood estimator.

*   **MU-MEMR Algorithm Steps:** A detailed algorithmic outline is provided, including initialization steps for Gaussian and Uniform parameters, and the iterative EM process with specific M-steps for updating Gaussian means/standard deviations and membership probabilities.

*   **Frequency Model for Risk Assessment:** The latter part introduces a frequency model that combines portfolio-level severity layers with trip-level layer frequencies. This model aims to create comparable risk indices across trips and drivers.

*   **Trip-Level Risk Index:** The concept of a trip-level risk index is introduced, utilizing aggregated wavelet coefficients and the defined severity layers. It defines "multi-layer tail counts" (MLTC) and proposes modeling these counts using a Poisson-Gamma conjugate prior for intensities, enabling sequential Bayesian updating.

structure.title: Frequency Model:
structure.summary:
This partial document, "4 Frequency Model," proposes a method for calculating trip- and driver-level risk indices. It combines portfolio-level severity layers (from a previous section) with trip-level frequency modeling. The core idea is to use the frequency of aggregated coefficients falling into different severity layers to form a joint frequency-severity risk rate.

Key points covered include:

*   **Trip-Level Risk Index:** This section details how to construct a trip-level risk index. It defines "exposure measure" ($E_i$) based on the number of retained wavelet coefficients for a trip. It then defines "multi-layer tail counts" ($N_{im}$) which count how many coefficients for a trip fall into each defined severity layer ($\Theta_m$).
*   **Modeling Frequency:** A Poisson model is used to represent these multi-layer tail counts, with an exposure offset ($E_i$) to account for different trip lengths. This allows for the estimation of per-exposure intensities ($\lambda_{im}$).
*   **Bayesian Updating:** Independent Gamma priors are assigned to the intensities ($\lambda_{im}$) for each severity layer. This choice of prior is conjugate to the Poisson likelihood, enabling closed-form Bayesian updating. This sequential updating capability is crucial for evolving driver-level risk indices as new trips occur.

nodes.title: Trip-Level Risk Index:
nodes.summary:
This partial document introduces a "Frequency Model" for assessing risk at both trip and driver levels. The core idea is to combine portfolio-level severity layers (from a previous section) with trip-level frequency data.

Key points covered include:

*   **Trip-Level Risk Index:**
    *   Defines "multi-layer tail counts" (MLTC) for each trip, which represent how often aggregated wavelet coefficients fall into different severity layers.
    *   Models these MLTCs using a Poisson distribution with an exposure offset.
    *   Employs Gamma priors for the intensity parameters, leveraging Poisson-Gamma conjugacy for Bayesian updating.
    *   Introduces "severity weights" that penalize layers based on their portfolio-level rarity, controlled by a parameter $\gamma$.
    *   Proposes a trip-level risk index ($S_i$) as a severity-weighted sum of layer-wise risk rates, which can be estimated via posterior means.

*   **Driver-Level Risk Index:**
    *   Extends the trip-level index to the driver level by sequentially updating the layer intensities ($\lambda_{dm}$) over a driver's trips.
    *   Uses conjugate Gamma posteriors for driver-specific intensities, allowing for closed-form updates as new trips arrive.
    *   The updated driver-level intensity is a weighted average of past experience and the new trip's empirical rate.
    *   Defines a driver-level risk index ($S_d^{(k)}$) as a severity-weighted sum of these sequentially updated driver-specific layer intensities, providing a time-evolving risk profile.

The document also briefly mentions an upcoming section (Section 5) that will apply this framework to a controlled dataset to examine driving patterns and evaluate the discriminative power of the proposed risk index in classification tasks.

structure.title: Application to Controlled Experiments:
structure.summary:
The provided document excerpt details a methodology for estimating driver risk profiles. It introduces a sequential update mechanism for driver risk indices, building upon a Poisson-Gamma model. The core idea is to estimate a driver's long-term risk profile by summarizing layer intensities after a series of trips using their posterior mean. This posterior mean is presented as a credibility representation that blends past accumulated history with new trip empirical rates, weighted by exposure.

The document then outlines how these updated layer intensities are used to estimate a driver-level risk index, which evolves over time and aggregates evidence from multiple trips. The trip-level index is presented as a special case of this driver-level index.

The latter part of the excerpt focuses on the application of this framework to a controlled experimental dataset (UAH-DriveSet). It describes the process of selecting the decomposition depth for wavelet coefficients, constructing a portfolio sample, and setting up the model components. The selection of the decomposition depth (J=6) is motivated by variance contribution analysis and visual inspection of coefficient trajectories. The document also explains the portfolio construction process, including hierarchical sampling and thinning to reduce serial dependence.

Furthermore, it details the fitting of a severity model using a Gaussian-Uniform mixture, explaining the choice of parameters and the interpretation of the fitted model. The fitted model separates typical driving dynamics (captured by Gaussian components) from abnormal patterns (captured by Uniform tail layers).

Finally, the excerpt discusses the estimation of trip- and driver-level risk indices by combining the frequency and severity models. It highlights how the multi-layer tail structure influences risk evaluation and how sequential updating aggregates evidence into a driver-level profile. The document illustrates how normal and risky trips are characterized by different MLTC totals and tail mass distributions, and how the proposed index accounts for exposure normalization and depth weighting.

nodes.title: Trip- and Driver-Level Risk Indices

The document details a sequential updating mechanism to create evolving driver-level risk profiles, illustrating how incorporating risky or normal trips affects the overall risk index. structure.title: Conclusion and Further Work
structure.summary: This partial document discusses a novel frequency-severity joint risk index for telematics signals, defining severity based on the rarity of abnormal driving patterns relative to a portfolio baseline. The paper's main contributions include formalizing a portfolio-level severity notion, extending existing models to a multi-uniform layered tail structure with a new fitting procedure, and developing a frequency model that yields a closed-form risk index and enables dynamic driver risk profiles. The study demonstrates that this severity weighting stabilizes and separates normal and risky driving behaviors, improving classification accuracy compared to frequency-only models. Future work directions include clustering abnormal patterns into event-level episodes for direct links to accident outcomes, explicitly modeling temporal dependence within trips, and extending the univariate index to a multivariate setting with multiple telematics signals. The proposed framework is presented as a foundational building block for various applications in insurance (risk assessment, dynamic pricing, driver profiling), transportation safety (risk mapping, intervention planning), and infrastructure planning, with potential for real-time risk scoring.
